library(cnvstrmliner)
library(GenomicRanges)
library(S4Vectors)
library(ggplot2)

logger::log_threshold(logger::WARN)

# Why this vignette exists

Once two CNV callers have been run over the same sample -- or the same caller
twice with different settings, or a caller against a simulated ground truth --
the obvious question is *how much do they agree?* The obvious answer, "count the
fraction of the genome where they say the same thing", is not a well defined one, and the
whole of this vignette is really an unpacking of why.

A segmentation makes two separate claims about a genome:

1. **Where the transitions are.** Where does one copy-number level stop and the
   next begin?
2. **What the levels are.** Is this piece amplified, deleted, or unchanged?

A caller can get one right and the other wrong, in either direction, and a
single agreement number cannot say which happened. Worse, most genomes are
mostly neutral, so a caller that reports *nothing at all* already agrees with
the truth over most of the genome. Any metric that gives that caller a good
score is measuring the composition of the sample, not the skill of the caller.

The functions described here are built around those two problems. They split the
"where" question from the "what" question, and every one of them is either
chance-corrected by construction or shipped with a companion that reports what
the do-nothing score would have been.

Each section below follows the same shape: what the metric measures, a picture
of the intuition, the code, when to reach for it, and what it leaves unanswered.

The tour runs in the order these are actually applied:

* **Part 1** -- is the bin-level data good enough to segment at all?
* **Parts 2 and 3** -- against a known truth, did the caller get the *levels*
  right, and did it get the *transitions* right?
* **Part 4** -- which of its individual segments can be believed?
* **Part 5** -- with no truth, what can a family of callers reveal about each
  other?
* **Part 6** -- whole-profile comparison in base pairs, on `cnvstrml` objects.
* **Part 7** -- picking among settings of one caller with information criteria.
* **Part 8** -- the rollups, and the single call that runs most of the above.

Parts 6 and 7 each end with a worked example of the metric preferring a caller
known to be the worst of the four. Those are the two most useful pages here.

# A worked example to measure

Everything in this vignette is computed on one small synthetic chromosome, so
that every number can be checked by eye against the picture.

## The reference and four callers

```{r toy-data}
makeSegmentation <- function(boundaries, states, chr = "chr1") {
  GRanges(
    seqnames = chr,
    ranges = IRanges(
      start = head(boundaries, -1) + 1,
      end = tail(boundaries, -1)
    ),
    cnv.annotation = states
  )
}

Mb <- 1e6

reference <- makeSegmentation(
  boundaries = c(0, 7, 13, 19, 23, 30) * Mb,
  states     = c("NEUT", "AMP", "NEUT", "HETDEL", "NEUT")
)

accurate <- makeSegmentation(
  boundaries = c(0, 7.25, 12.80, 19.15, 22.80, 30) * Mb,
  states     = c("NEUT", "AMP", "NEUT", "HETDEL", "NEUT")
)

fragmented <- makeSegmentation(
  boundaries = c(
    0, 3.4, 7.1, 9.2, 9.9, 12.9, 15.5,
    19.1, 21.0, 22.9, 26.2, 30
  ) * Mb,
  states = c(
    "NEUT", "NEUT", "AMP", "NEUT", "AMP", "NEUT",
    "NEUT", "HETDEL", "HETDEL", "NEUT", "NEUT"
  )
)

conservative <- makeSegmentation(
  boundaries = c(0, 8.5, 11.5, 30) * Mb,
  states     = c("NEUT", "AMP", "NEUT")
)

shifted <- makeSegmentation(
  boundaries = c(0, 5.4, 11.3, 20.6, 24.4, 30) * Mb,
  states     = c("NEUT", "AMP", "NEUT", "HETDEL", "NEUT")
)

callers <- list(
  "Accurate caller"     = accurate,
  "Fragmented caller"   = fragmented,
  "Conservative caller" = conservative,
  "Shifted caller"      = shifted
)
```

The four callers are caricatures, each exaggerating one realistic failure mode:

* **Accurate caller** -- finds both events, with boundaries a couple of hundred
  kilobases off. This is what a good result looks like.
* **Fragmented caller** -- finds both events but chops them into pieces, and
  inserts a spurious neutral gap in the middle of the amplification.
  Over-segmentation.
* **Conservative caller** -- reports a smaller amplification and misses the
  deletion entirely. Under-calling.
* **Shifted caller** -- reports exactly the right *events* but places every
  boundary one to two megabases away. Right biology, wrong coordinates.

## The evidence grid

Every bin-level metric in the package needs to be told **where the assay could
see anything**. On whole-genome data that is the whole genome and a uniform
tiling is fine. On a capture panel it is the target regions, and this matters a
great deal: tiling a whole-exome sample uniformly puts most tiles in
unsequenced intergenic space where no caller had evidence, which ends up
measuring agreement over territory nobody looked at.

This toy assay is a capture panel: 100 kb targets every 200 kb, with a two
megabase capture desert between 15 and 17 Mb.

```{r targets}
target_starts <- seq(1, 30 * Mb, by = 0.2 * Mb)
targets <- GRanges(
  seqnames = "chr1",
  ranges   = IRanges(start = target_starts, width = 0.1 * Mb)
)
targets <- targets[!(start(targets) > 15 * Mb & end(targets) < 17 * Mb)]

length(targets)
```

## The same segmentations as `cnvstrml` objects

The bin-level metrics in Parts 2 to 5 accept bare `GRanges`, which is why the
toy data above is enough for them. A second group of metrics -- the whole-profile
comparisons of Part 6 -- works on `cnvstrml` objects instead, because they read
allele copy numbers and log-ratios rather than just a state label.

Promoting the toy segmentations, they are `cnvstrml` objects that require
`total.allele.copies`, `major.allele.copies`, `minor.allele.copies`, `cnv.lrr`,
`cnv.markers`, `cnv.totalmarkers` and `cnv.cf` on its segments, so a consistent
set is invented from each state label.

```{r cnvstrml-objects}
state_cn <- data.frame(
  cnv.annotation      = c("NEUT", "AMP", "HETDEL", "HOMDEL"),
  total.allele.copies = c(2, 4, 1, 0),
  major.allele.copies = c(1, 3, 1, 0),
  minor.allele.copies = c(1, 1, 0, 0),
  cnv.lrr             = c(0, 1.0, -1.0, -3.0)
)

asCnvstrml <- function(gr, method) {
  i <- match(gr$cnv.annotation, state_cn$cnv.annotation)
  mcols(gr) <- cbind(mcols(gr), state_cn[i, -1, drop = FALSE])
  gr$cnv.markers <- pmax(1, round(width(gr) / 2e5))
  gr$cnv.totalmarkers <- gr$cnv.markers
  gr$cnv.cf <- 1
  new("cnvstrml",
    segments = gr, sample = "toy", method = method,
    genome = "hg38", sex = "XX", purity = 0.8, ploidy = 2
  )
}

reference_obj <- asCnvstrml(reference, "reference")
caller_objs <- mapply(asCnvstrml, callers, names(callers))
```

## Bin-level log-ratio data

The input-quality metrics of Part 1 and the information criteria of Part 7 never
look at segments alone -- they need the per-bin log-ratios the segmentation was
fitted to. The chunk below simulates a `.cnr`-style table: bins of 100 kb,
drawn around the true state mean with a realistic amount of noise. This is
typically a file obtained by running CNVkit on a pair or tumor - matched normal
or a tumor - PON set.

```{r bin-data}
set.seed(42)

bins <- GRanges(
  seqnames = "chr1",
  ranges   = IRanges(start = seq(1, 30 * Mb, by = 1e5), width = 1e5)
)

state_mean <- c(NEUT = 0, AMP = 0.9, HETDEL = -0.85)
true_state <- assignBinState(bins, reference)
mu <- state_mean[true_state]
mu[is.na(mu)] <- 0

bins$log2 <- rnorm(length(bins), mean = mu, sd = 0.18)
bins$weight <- 1

cnr <- data.frame(
  chromosome = as.character(seqnames(bins)),
  start      = start(bins),
  log2       = bins$log2,
  depth      = pmax(1, rnbinom(length(bins), mu = 120, size = 8))
)

head(cnr, 3)
```

## Plotting helpers

These are only for the figures in this vignette; they are not part of the
package.

```{r plot-helpers}
state_colours <- c(
  NEUT   = "grey82",
  AMP    = "#D7301F",
  HETDEL = "#2B8CBE",
  HOMDEL = "#08306B"
)

theme_slide <- function(base_size = 15) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
      # Titles here are full sentences; at the default title size (1.2 * base_size)
      # the longer ones run past the edge of the device and get clipped. Shrinking
      # them relative to the base size, and letting the title span the whole plot
      # rather than only the panel, keeps them readable and complete.
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = rel(0.85)),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey30", size = rel(0.75)),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.title = element_blank(),
      axis.title.y = element_blank()
    )
}

trackFrame <- function(track_list) {
  rows <- lapply(names(track_list), function(nm) {
    d <- as.data.frame(track_list[[nm]])
    d$Segmentation <- nm
    d
  })
  d <- dplyr::bind_rows(rows)
  d$Segmentation <- factor(d$Segmentation, levels = rev(names(track_list)))
  d$row <- as.numeric(d$Segmentation)
  d
}

plotTracks <- function(track_list, title = NULL, subtitle = NULL) {
  d <- trackFrame(track_list)
  ggplot(d) +
    geom_rect(
      aes(
        xmin = start / Mb, xmax = end / Mb,
        ymin = row - 0.36, ymax = row + 0.36,
        fill = cnv.annotation
      ),
      colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = state_colours) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      breaks = seq_along(levels(d$Segmentation)),
      labels = levels(d$Segmentation)
    ) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle, x = "Position on chr1 (Mb)") +
    theme_slide()
}
```

Part 4 reuses the track layout of Figure 1, but with the segments shaded by a
per-segment score rather than by state. That needs two colour scales in one
picture, so those figures are two aligned panels stacked with `r CRANpkg("patchwork")`: the
reference states on top, the scored segmentations underneath.

```{r plot-helpers-scored}
library(patchwork)

xlim_chr <- scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 30), expand = c(0.01, 0))

# Track figures carry wide y-axis labels, which push the panel -- and with it the
# left-aligned title -- to the right. Wrap long captions so they are not clipped.
wrapSub <- function(x, width = 62) {
  if (is.null(x)) {
    return(NULL)
  }
  paste(strwrap(x, width = width), collapse = "\n")
}

refPanel <- function(title = NULL, subtitle = NULL) {
  plotTracks(list("Reference truth" = reference),
    title = title, subtitle = wrapSub(subtitle)
  ) +
    xlim_chr + labs(x = NULL) +
    # The state colour code is already established by Figure 1, and a legend here
    # would sit between the two panels and break them apart.
    theme(
      legend.position = "none",
      axis.text.x = element_blank(), plot.margin = margin(b = 2)
    )
}

scorePanel <- function(scored_list, score_col, score_name) {
  d <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(scored_list), function(nm) {
    x <- as.data.frame(scored_list[[nm]])
    x$score <- mcols(scored_list[[nm]])[[score_col]]
    x$Segmentation <- nm
    x[, c("start", "end", "score", "Segmentation")]
  }))
  d$Segmentation <- factor(d$Segmentation, levels = rev(names(scored_list)))
  d$row <- as.numeric(d$Segmentation)

  ggplot(d) +
    geom_rect(
      aes(
        xmin = start / Mb, xmax = end / Mb,
        ymin = row - 0.36, ymax = row + 0.36, fill = score
      ),
      colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4
    ) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(
      low = "#D7301F", mid = "#FEE08B", high = "#1A9850",
      midpoint = 0.5, limits = c(0, 1),
      name = score_name, na.value = "grey92"
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      breaks = seq_along(levels(d$Segmentation)),
      labels = levels(d$Segmentation)
    ) +
    xlim_chr +
    labs(x = "Position on chr1 (Mb)") +
    theme_slide() +
    guides(fill = guide_colourbar(
      title.position = "top", title.hjust = 0.5,
      barwidth = grid::unit(12, "lines"),
      barheight = grid::unit(0.7, "lines")
    )) +
    theme(legend.title = element_text(), plot.margin = margin(t = 2))
}

scoredTrackFigure <- function(scored_list, score_col, score_name,
                              title = NULL, subtitle = NULL) {
  refPanel(title, subtitle) /
    scorePanel(scored_list, score_col, score_name) +
    plot_layout(heights = c(1, length(scored_list) * 0.95))
}
```

```{r fig-overview, fig.height = 5.2, fig.cap = "The reference segmentation and the four callers scored throughout this vignette."}
plotTracks(
  c(list("Reference truth" = reference), callers),
  title = "One chromosome, one truth, four ways to get it wrong",
  subtitle = "Red = amplification, blue = heterozygous deletion, grey = neutral"
)
```

# Part 1 -- Is the input good enough to segment at all?

Every metric in Parts 2 to 8 compares segmentations. None of them can reveal
that the *data* was too noisy to segment in the first place -- a caller handed
unusable bins will produce a segmentation, and two callers handed the same
unusable bins will often agree with each other about it.

The two functions here look at the bin-level signal directly, before any
segmentation exists. They take a plain data frame rather than a `cnvstrml`
object, because they are meant to run on a caller's raw bin output (a CNVkit
`.cnr` file, for instance).

## `computeMAPD()` -- how noisy are the bins?

### What it measures

The median absolute difference between *adjacent* bins, within each chromosome.
Because neighbouring bins almost always belong to the same copy-number segment,
their true difference is zero nearly everywhere; whatever difference is
observed is technical noise. Taking the median rather than the mean is what stops
the handful of real transitions from inflating the estimate.

Lower is better. MAPD is the standard first-pass quality gate for array and
capture copy-number data, and the number a caller's own defaults are usually
tuned against.

### Intuition

```{r fig-mapd, fig.height = 4.6, fig.cap = "Two samples with the same underlying copy-number profile. MAPD measures the bin-to-bin scatter, which is what makes the second one unsegmentable, and ignores the two real transitions."}
noisy <- cnr
noisy$log2 <- rnorm(nrow(cnr), mean = mu, sd = 0.55)

mapd_frame <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  transform(cnr, Sample = sprintf("Clean  (MAPD = %.3f)", computeMAPD(cnr))),
  transform(noisy, Sample = sprintf("Noisy  (MAPD = %.3f)", computeMAPD(noisy)))
)

ggplot(mapd_frame, aes(x = start / Mb, y = log2)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.7, colour = "grey35", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = c(7, 13, 19, 23), linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "#2B8CBE", linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~Sample, ncol = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "The same profile, three times the noise",
    subtitle = wrapSub("Blue dashed lines are the true transitions. MAPD does not count them."),
    x = "Position on chr1 (Mb)", y = "Bin log ratio"
  ) +
  theme_slide() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 90))
```

### How to use it

```{r mapd-use}
computeMAPD(cnr)
computeMAPD(noisy)
```

The input must be a data frame with a `chromosome` column and either `log2`
(the default, `use_log = TRUE`) or `depth` (`use_log = FALSE`). Grouping by
`chromosome` matters: without it, the last bin of one chromosome is differenced
against the first bin of the next, which manufactures a large artificial jump
per chromosome.

### When to use it

As a gate, before anything downstream is trusted. A sample whose MAPD is far
above the cohort median will over-segment under any caller and any setting, and
no amount of comparison metric will fix that -- it is a sequencing problem, not
a segmentation problem.

### Advantages and limitations

* Needs no truth, no segmentation, and no reference sample.
* Insensitive to real copy-number changes, which is what makes it a noise
  measure rather than a complexity measure.
* But it is scale-dependent: MAPD on log-ratios and MAPD on raw depths are not
  comparable, and neither is comparable across bin sizes. Fix the bin width
  before comparing samples.
* It says nothing about *where* the noise is. A sample can have an acceptable
  global MAPD and one catastrophically noisy chromosome.

## `computeGini()` -- how uneven is the coverage?

### What it measures

The Gini coefficient of the coverage distribution across bins: 0 means every bin
was sequenced to exactly the same depth, and values approaching 1 mean the reads
piled into a small fraction of the bins. It is the same statistic used for
income inequality, applied to depth.

MAPD and Gini fail on different samples. MAPD catches *noisy* data; Gini catches
*unevenly captured* data, where some targets are deep enough to call and others
have almost no reads. A capture panel with poor uniformity can have a
respectable MAPD over the bins that worked.

### Intuition

```{r fig-gini, fig.height = 4.2, fig.cap = "Two coverage distributions with the same mean depth. The Gini coefficient separates them; the mean does not."}
even <- pmax(1, rnbinom(nrow(cnr), mu = 120, size = 40))
uneven <- pmax(1, rnbinom(nrow(cnr), mu = 120, size = 0.7))

gini_frame <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  data.frame(
    depth = even,
    Sample = sprintf(
      "Even    (Gini = %.3f)",
      computeGini(data.frame(depth = even))
    )
  ),
  data.frame(
    depth = uneven,
    Sample = sprintf(
      "Uneven  (Gini = %.3f)",
      computeGini(data.frame(depth = uneven))
    )
  )
)

ggplot(gini_frame, aes(x = depth, fill = Sample)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 45, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~Sample, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#1A9850", "#D7301F")) +
  labs(
    title = "Same mean depth, different usable fraction",
    subtitle = wrapSub("Both distributions average about 120x; only one of them can be called everywhere"),
    x = "Depth per bin", y = "Bins"
  ) +
  theme_slide() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 90, margin = margin(r = 10))
  )
```

### How to use it

```{r gini-use}
computeGini(cnr)
```

The default `use_log = FALSE` reads a `depth` column, and that is the option to
use. `use_log = TRUE` runs the same calculation on the `log2` column, but the
Gini coefficient is only defined for non-negative quantities and log-ratios are
routinely negative, so the result is not interpretable as an inequality measure:

```{r gini-log-caution}
# Runs, but the result is not an inequality coefficient at all: because log
# ratios are signed, it is not even bounded by 1.
computeGini(cnr, use_log = TRUE)
```

A Gini coefficient above 1 is the tell. Use `use_log = FALSE` on depths.

### When to use it

On capture and amplicon panels, alongside MAPD, as part of the same gate. Track
it across a batch: a jump in Gini usually means a library-prep or hybridisation
problem, and it will show up here before it shows up in anybody's segment calls.

### Advantages and limitations

* Single, bounded, cohort-comparable number that summarises capture uniformity.
* Independent of mean depth, so it separates "shallow" from "uneven" -- two
  problems with completely different remedies.
* Blind to position, exactly like MAPD. It does not identify *which* targets
  failed; for that, filter the bins on depth directly.
* Meaningless on signed input -- see the caution above.

## `computeCoverage()` -- per-target depth from a BAM

### What it measures

Mean read depth over each region of a BED file, read straight from an indexed
BAM with `bamsignals`. This is the function that produces the `depth` column the
other two consume, when no caller bin file is already available.

### How to use it

```{r coverage-use, eval = FALSE}
cov <- computeCoverage(
  bamfile = "sample.bam",
  bedfile = "targets.bed"
)

computeGini(cov)
computeMAPD(cov, use_log = FALSE)
```

This chunk is not evaluated -- it needs a real indexed BAM, which the package
does not ship. The BAM must be coordinate-sorted and indexed, and the BED
contig names must match the BAM header.

### When to use it

Only when no bin-level output is available to start from. If the caller already
emits a `.cnr`, `.cnn` or equivalent, use that: it has been corrected for GC and
target efficiency, and this function has not.

# Part 2 -- Did the caller get the copy number right?

## `assignBinState()` -- the projection everything is built on

### What it does

Every bin-level metric works the same way underneath: each bin is handed to the
one segment it overlaps most, and inherits that segment's state. Bins that no
segment covers are `NA`. `assignBinState()` exposes that projection.

### Intuition

```{r fig-assign, fig.height = 4.4, fig.cap = "Each target is coloured by the state of the segment that covers most of it. Targets no segment covers are left blank -- they are never silently treated as neutral."}
bin_states <- data.frame(
  start = start(targets),
  end = end(targets),
  Truth = assignBinState(targets, reference),
  Accurate = assignBinState(targets, accurate),
  Fragmented = assignBinState(targets, fragmented)
)

bin_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(
  bin_states,
  cols = c("Truth", "Accurate", "Fragmented"),
  names_to = "Segmentation", values_to = "State"
)
bin_long$Segmentation <- factor(bin_long$Segmentation,
  levels = c("Fragmented", "Accurate", "Truth")
)
bin_long$row <- as.numeric(bin_long$Segmentation)

ggplot(bin_long) +
  geom_rect(
    aes(
      xmin = start / Mb, xmax = end / Mb,
      ymin = row - 0.36, ymax = row + 0.36, fill = State
    ),
    colour = NA
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = state_colours, na.value = "white") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:3, labels = levels(bin_long$Segmentation)) +
  labs(
    title = "A segmentation, projected onto the capture targets",
    subtitle = "The white stripe at 15-17 Mb is the capture desert: no target, no evidence, no score",
    x = "Position on chr1 (Mb)"
  ) +
  theme_slide()
```

### How to use it

```{r assign-use}
truth_states <- assignBinState(targets, reference)
table(truth_states, useNA = "ifany")
```

The reason to call it directly is speed. When one reference is scored against
many segmentations -- a forty-setting parameter sweep, say -- compute the
reference projection once and hand it to `annotateBinStateConcordance()` through
its `reference_state` argument instead of letting every comparison recompute it.

### Advantages and limitations

* **Advantage:** one bin, one segment. This makes bin sets true sets, so unions
  and intersections downstream are honest.
* **Limitation:** a bin straddling a real transition is forced to one side. Bins
  much wider than the features of interest will blur them; keep the grid at
  or below the resolution of the assay.

## `computeStateKappa()` -- chance-corrected state agreement

### What it measures

The single most useful "how good is this call set" number in the package.
Cohen's kappa compares the state assigned to each bin by the query and by the
reference, and then subtracts the agreement expected by luck given how
much of each state each side reports:

$$\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}$$

where $p_o$ is the observed agreement and $p_e$ the agreement expected if the
two label sets were thrown down independently.

### Intuition

The point of the correction is visible directly. A caller that labels the whole
genome neutral agrees with the reference over `r round(100 * mean(assignBinState(targets, reference) == "NEUT", na.rm = TRUE))`%
of the targets -- a raw agreement that looks like competence and is not. Kappa
scores that caller at exactly zero.

```{r fig-kappa, fig.height = 4.6, fig.cap = "Raw agreement flatters every caller, including the one that does nothing. Kappa does not."}
null_score <- scoreNullCaller(reference, bins = targets)

kappa_tbl <- bind_rows(lapply(names(callers), function(nm) {
  k <- computeStateKappa(callers[[nm]], reference, bins = targets)
  data.frame(
    Caller = nm, `Raw agreement` = k$p_o, Kappa = k$kappa,
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}))
kappa_tbl <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(
    Caller = "Do-nothing caller",
    `Raw agreement` = null_score$null_p_o,
    Kappa = null_score$null_kappa, check.names = FALSE
  ),
  kappa_tbl
)

kappa_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(kappa_tbl, -Caller,
  names_to = "Score", values_to = "Value"
)
kappa_long$Caller <- factor(kappa_long$Caller, levels = rev(kappa_tbl$Caller))

ggplot(kappa_long, aes(x = Value, y = Caller, fill = Score)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.65) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Raw agreement" = "grey70", "Kappa" = "#2B8CBE")) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(min(0, min(kappa_long$Value)), 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Why raw agreement is not a quality score",
    subtitle = "The do-nothing caller earns a high raw agreement and a kappa of zero",
    x = "Score"
  ) +
  theme_slide()
```

### How to use it

```{r kappa-use}
k <- computeStateKappa(accurate, reference, bins = targets)
k$kappa
k$n_bins_scored
k$n_bins_unscored
head(k$marginals)
```

`marginals` is worth looking at whenever a kappa is surprising. It shows how
much of each state each side called, and a low kappa driven by a lopsided
marginal is a composition artefact rather than a segmentation failure.

Two arguments change the question being asked:

* `statecol = "total.allele.copies"` scores integer copy number instead of the
  `AMP`/`NEUT`/`HETDEL` label -- a stricter test.
* `simplify = TRUE` collapses `HETDEL` and `HOMDEL` into a single `DEL`, and
  strips the `-LOH` suffixes, matching what `cnvMetrics()` does. The default is
  `FALSE` here on purpose: the homozygous/heterozygous distinction is usually
  the one that matters most.

### When to use it

Reach for kappa first, every time, whenever a trusted reference is available and
one number per caller is wanted. It is the right ranking statistic for a
benchmark table or a parameter sweep.

Conventional reading of the value (Landis and Koch): above 0.8 almost perfect,
0.6--0.8 substantial, 0.4--0.6 moderate, 0.2--0.4 fair, below 0.2 barely
distinguishable from doing nothing. A **negative** kappa in CNV work almost
always means a purity or ploidy solution has flipped, not that segmentation
failed.

### Advantages

* Immune to the neutral-genome baseline, which is the failure mode that ruins
  every naive agreement score.
* One number, standard, comparable across samples and across studies.
* Reports how many bins it could not score, making it obvious when it is quietly
  answering a narrower question than the one posed.

### Limitations

* It merges the two error directions. A caller that misses events and a caller
  that invents them can score the same kappa; use `computeEventRecovery()` to
  separate them.
* It is blind to segment identity. A caller that splits every reference segment
  in half but states both halves correctly scores a perfect 1.0. That is a
  feature when only copy number matters, and a trap when breakpoints matter
  -- see Part 3.
* Kappa depends on the marginals, so values from samples with very different
  altered fractions are only loosely comparable.

## `scoreNullCaller()` -- the floor any score has to beat

### What it measures

It builds the caller that emits nothing -- one neutral call over every bin the
reference covers -- and scores it. Nothing about a real segmentation is
involved. It is a property of the *sample*.

### Intuition

```{r fig-null, fig.height = 3.6, fig.cap = "Raw agreement achieved by a caller that reports the whole genome as neutral. The do-nothing baseline varies enormously between samples: a raw agreement of 0.80 is excellent on a heavily rearranged genome and worse than useless on a quiet one."}
quiet_reference <- makeSegmentation(
  boundaries = c(0, 26, 28, 30) * Mb,
  states     = c("NEUT", "AMP", "NEUT")
)
busy_reference <- makeSegmentation(
  boundaries = c(0, 4, 9, 14, 18, 24, 30) * Mb,
  states     = c("AMP", "NEUT", "HETDEL", "AMP", "HETDEL", "AMP")
)

null_tbl <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(
    Sample = "Quiet genome",
    Baseline = scoreNullCaller(quiet_reference, bins = targets)$null_p_o
  ),
  data.frame(
    Sample = "Our example",
    Baseline = scoreNullCaller(reference, bins = targets)$null_p_o
  ),
  data.frame(
    Sample = "Heavily rearranged genome",
    Baseline = scoreNullCaller(busy_reference, bins = targets)$null_p_o
  )
)
null_tbl$Sample <- factor(null_tbl$Sample, levels = rev(null_tbl$Sample))

ggplot(null_tbl, aes(x = Baseline, y = Sample)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey65", width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Baseline)), hjust = -0.2, size = 5) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.08)) +
  labs(
    title = "What doing nothing scores, per sample",
    x = "Raw agreement of the do-nothing caller"
  ) +
  theme_slide()
```

### How to use it

```{r null-use}
null_score <- scoreNullCaller(reference, bins = targets)
null_score$null_p_o
null_score$null_kappa
```

### When to use it

Print it next to any raw-agreement or "fraction of genome concordant" figure
being reported, including ones produced outside this package. It also serves as a
sanity check on a pipeline: `null_kappa` must come out at zero, and it is
computed rather than asserted precisely so that a bug in the state handling
shows up here instead of hiding inside every real score.

### Advantages and limitations

* **Advantage:** turns "is 0.78 good?" from an unanswerable question into an
  answerable one.
* **Limitation:** it is a diagnostic, not a metric. There is nothing to rank
  with it, and reporting it as a caller's score would be meaningless.

## `computeStateConfusion()` -- which states get confused for which

### What it measures

The contingency table kappa is computed from, plus per-state recall, precision
and F1. Kappa says how much better than chance; this says *where the mistakes
are*.

### Intuition

```{r fig-confusion, fig.height = 4.4, fig.cap = "Rows are the state in the reference, columns the state the caller assigned, and counts are targets. The conservative caller does not merely score lower -- it fails in a specific way: deletions are called neutral."}
cm <- computeStateConfusion(conservative, reference, bins = targets)

ggplot(cm$counts, aes(x = query_state, y = subject_state, fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), size = 5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "grey95", high = "#2B8CBE", guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Where the conservative caller loses the deletion",
    x = "Called by the caller", y = "True state"
  ) +
  theme_slide() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 90), panel.grid = element_blank())
```

The off-diagonal cell in the `HETDEL` row is the whole story: every deleted
target was called neutral.

### How to use it

```{r confusion-use}
cm$per_state
```

`recall` is, of the targets the reference calls this state, the fraction the
caller agreed on. `precision` is the converse. `support_subject` and
`support_query` are the two marginals -- always check them, because a recall
computed over four targets is not evidence of anything.

### When to use it

As the immediate follow-up whenever a kappa is disappointing and the reason
matters before changing a parameter. Also when the states are not equally
important: a caller with poor overall kappa but excellent `HOMDEL`
recall may be exactly the right tool for finding tumour-suppressor losses.

### Advantages

* Diagnostic rather than merely evaluative -- it points at a fix.
* Per-state, so rare but clinically important states are not drowned out by the
  neutral majority.

### Limitations

* Not a single number, so it cannot rank callers.
* Per-state rates over small supports are noisy.
* Like kappa, it is entirely blind to how the genome was cut up.

## `computeEventRecovery()` -- missed events versus invented ones

### What it measures

Two numbers that kappa merges into one:

* **recall** -- of the genuinely altered territory in the reference, how much
  did the caller find?
* **precision** -- of what the caller called altered, how much is real?

A segment counts as recovered when at least `concordance_threshold` (default
half) of its targets carry the matching state, so overlapping a real event while
calling the wrong copy number does not earn credit. Segments are weighted by
width by default, so a chromosome-arm event is not traded off against a focal
one.

### Intuition

```{r fig-recovery, fig.height = 4.6, fig.cap = "The same information kappa compresses into one number, split into the two directions that call for opposite fixes. Bottom right: finds everything and more. Top left: everything it says is right, but it says little."}
rec_tbl <- bind_rows(lapply(names(callers), function(nm) {
  r <- computeEventRecovery(callers[[nm]], reference, bins = targets)
  data.frame(
    Caller = nm, Recall = r$recall_altered,
    Precision = r$precision_altered
  )
}))

ggplot(rec_tbl, aes(x = Recall, y = Precision, label = Caller)) +
  geom_point(size = 5, colour = "#D7301F") +
  geom_text(vjust = -1.1, size = 4.6) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey70") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.25, 1.25)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.05, 1.20)) +
  annotate("text",
    x = 1.0, y = 0.05, label = "over-calling",
    colour = "grey40", size = 4.5
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = 0.12, y = 1.1, label = "under-calling",
    colour = "grey40", size = 4.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Recall and precision on altered regions",
    x = "Recall (of real events, how many were found)",
    y = "Precision (of calls made, how many are real)"
  ) +
  theme_slide() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 90))
```

### How to use it

```{r recovery-use}
rec <- computeEventRecovery(conservative, reference, bins = targets)
rec[c(
  "recall_altered", "precision_altered", "sorensen",
  "n_truth_altered", "n_query_altered"
)]
```

### When to use it

Whenever the fix depends on the direction of the error -- which, in practice, is
whenever a sensitivity knob is being turned. Low recall wants a more sensitive
setting; low precision wants a less sensitive one; a single score cannot say
which knob to turn or which way.

### Advantages

* Directional, and therefore actionable.
* Width-weighted, so large events are not outvoted by focal ones.
* Segments carrying no target at all are excluded from both numerator and
  denominator, and counted separately as `n_truth_unscorable` /
  `n_query_unscorable`. A caller is not charged for events lying entirely
  between capture targets, which it could not have seen.

### Limitations

* The recall reported is a **raw** recall, not an attainable one. It excludes
  events with no evidence geometrically, but not events too faint to detect at
  the sample's purity. On a low-purity sample it will make every caller look
  worse than it deserves.
* `concordance_threshold` is a choice, and a segment at 0.49 and one at 0.51 are
  treated as opposites.
* Not chance-corrected. Read it alongside kappa, not instead of it.

## `getBinJaccardIndex()` -- the same Jaccard, counted in bins

### What it measures

Exactly what `getJaccardIndex()` in Part 6 measures -- the overlap of the altered
genome between two segmentations -- with the sets counted in bins of the evidence
grid instead of in base pairs. Same formula, same definition of a true positive,
same field names with `_bins` in place of `_bp`.

Every bin is given the state of the segment covering most of it, on both sides. A
bin is then **altered in the query** if its query state is not neutral, **altered
in the subject** if its subject state is not neutral, and a **true positive** if
it is altered on both sides *and* both sides give it the same label:

$$J = \frac{TP}{S + Q - TP}, \qquad D = \frac{2\,TP}{S + Q}$$

Requiring the same label is what makes it the analogue of the base-pair function,
where a region contributes to `tp` only when it is non-neutral on both sides and
carries `status == "TP"`. A bin called `AMP` by one side and `HETDEL` by the other
is in the union and not in the intersection, so it lowers the score twice over.

Bins that no segment covers on one or both sides are in neither set: they are
excluded from the intersection and from the union alike, never imputed to
neutral.

### Intuition

On a uniform grid the two versions agree closely, which is the first thing to
check -- it is the same formula, so they should. The divergence appears exactly
where the grid is not uniform.

```{r fig-binjaccard, fig.height = 4.8, fig.cap = "Bin-based and base-pair Jaccard for the four callers, plus a fifth constructed to make the two disagree. The first four agree to within 0.02. The desert-spanning caller claims 2.6 Mb of extra amplification of which only 3 targets carry evidence, and the base-pair version charges it almost four times as much as the bin version."}
# Constructed for this comparison only: the accurate caller plus a spurious
# amplification laid across the 15-17 Mb capture desert.
desert_caller <- makeSegmentation(
  boundaries = c(0, 7.25, 12.80, 14.8, 17.4, 19.15, 22.80, 30) * Mb,
  states     = c("NEUT", "AMP", "NEUT", "AMP", "NEUT", "HETDEL", "NEUT")
)

jac_set <- c(callers, list("Desert-spanning caller" = desert_caller))

jac_compare <- bind_rows(lapply(names(jac_set), function(nm) {
  b <- getBinJaccardIndex(jac_set[[nm]], reference, bins = targets)
  p <- getJaccardIndex(compareSegmentStatus(
    asCnvstrml(jac_set[[nm]], nm), reference_obj
  ))
  data.frame(
    Caller = nm,
    `Bins (getBinJaccardIndex)`    = b$jaccard_bin,
    `Base pairs (getJaccardIndex)` = p$jaccard,
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}))

jac_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(jac_compare, -Caller,
                               names_to = "Unit", values_to = "Jaccard")
jac_long$Caller <- factor(jac_long$Caller, levels = rev(names(jac_set)))

ggplot(jac_long, aes(x = Jaccard, y = Caller, fill = Unit)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Jaccard)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), hjust = -0.15, size = 4.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.15), breaks = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Bins (getBinJaccardIndex)"    = "#2B8CBE",
    "Base pairs (getJaccardIndex)" = "grey45"
  )) +
  labs(title = "The same coefficient on two different units",
       subtitle = wrapSub("They agree until the unsequenced genome starts carrying weight"),
       x = "Jaccard index of the altered genome") +
  theme_slide() +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

For the four callers the two agree to within 0.02, and the conservative caller
lands on 0.30 either way. That is the expected result: the toy panel tiles the
chromosome evenly, so counting bins and counting base pairs are nearly
proportional, and any disagreement would mean one of the two was computing
something else.

The fifth caller is the point. It is the accurate caller plus a spurious
amplification from 14.8 to 17.4 Mb -- 2.6 Mb of extra altered territory, of which
only **3 targets** carry any evidence, because the capture desert runs from 15 to
17 Mb. The base-pair Jaccard falls from 0.92 to **0.73**; the bin Jaccard falls
from 0.90 to only **0.85**. The base-pair version charges nearly four times as
much for a mistake that is mostly in territory nobody sequenced.

Which of those two is right depends on the assay, and that is the whole decision:

* On **capture or amplicon** data, take the bin answer. The caller cannot be
  credited or charged for a region with no reads, and `bins = targets` is what
  restricts both sets to the evidence.
* On **whole-genome** data every base carries evidence, the two converge, and
  `getJaccardIndex()` is the cheaper call.

### How to use it

```{r binjaccard-use}
bj <- getBinJaccardIndex(conservative, reference, bins = targets)

unlist(bj)
```

The field names are those of `getJaccardIndex()`, with `_n` marking the three
counts as numbers of bins where the base-pair version writes `_bp`. The two
unitless fractions keep their names unchanged, so a report can switch units
without renaming anything.

Read the counts before the coefficient. `subject_altered_genome_n` and
`query_altered_genome_n` are the two set sizes and `tp_altered_genome_n` their
agreeing intersection, so the conservative caller's 15 against 50 says
immediately that it is reporting less than a third of the altered genome. The two
directional fractions decompose the Jaccard exactly as they do in base pairs:

* `matched_query_altered_genome` is a **precision** -- of the bins this caller
  calls altered, the fraction the reference agrees about;
* `matched_subject_altered_genome` is a **recall**.

### When to use it

Whenever a single altered-genome overlap number is wanted on target-based data.
Report it with its two directional fractions rather than alone: the conservative
caller's Jaccard of 0.30 comes from a precision of 1.00 and a recall of 0.30,
which is a completely different diagnosis from the shifted caller's 0.52 built
out of 0.69 and 0.68.

### Advantages

* Same formula and field names as `getJaccardIndex()` -- only the `_bp` counts
  become `_n` -- so switching units does not mean reinterpreting the output.
* Excludes the neutral genome, so there is no credit for calling nothing -- the
  problem Part 2 opens with.
* Bins no segment covers are excluded from both sets, so a caller is neither
  rewarded nor punished for placing segments in deserts.
* `sorensen_bin` is returned alongside, for reports that use Dice.

### Limitations

* Resolution is the bin grid. Two segmentations differing by less than a target
  spacing are indistinguishable, and a bin straddling a real transition is
  assigned wholly to one side.
* Requires states to match exactly, so a caller that finds every event but
  systematically calls `HETDEL` where the truth says `HOMDEL` scores near zero.
  Pass `simplify = TRUE` to pool the deletion states when that distinction is not
  the question.
* Not chance-corrected, and it says nothing about position or fragmentation
  beyond what the bin overlap captures. Read it with `computeStateKappa()` and
  `computeFragmentation()`.
* Not numerically identical to `getJaccardIndex()` even on whole-genome data: the
  base-pair version derives its true positives from `compareSegmentStatus()`
  status labels, this one from per-bin state equality.

# Part 3 -- Did the caller cut the genome in the right places?

Everything in Part 2 is blind to segment identity: split a reference segment in
two, state both halves correctly, and kappa is still 1.0. The metrics here ask
the complementary question, and are correspondingly blind to state.

## `getSegmentBreakpoints()` and `computeBoundaryConcordance()`

### What they measure

`getSegmentBreakpoints()` reduces a segmentation to the set of positions where
it transitions. `computeBoundaryConcordance()` then scores one such set against
another, counting a called breakpoint as correct when a reference breakpoint
lies within `tolerance_bp`.

The first and last position on each chromosome are dropped by default. They
record where the segmentation happened to start and stop -- usually the first
and last covered target -- rather than a detected transition, and counting them
inflates the agreement between any two segmentations of the same assay.

### Intuition

```{r fig-boundary, fig.height = 4.6, fig.cap = "A breakpoint counts as found if a real one lies inside its tolerance window. The shifted caller finds the right events and none of the right boundaries."}
all_tracks <- c(list("Reference truth" = reference), callers)
bp_frame <- bind_rows(lapply(names(all_tracks), function(nm) {
  data.frame(
    Segmentation = nm,
    pos = start(getSegmentBreakpoints(all_tracks[[nm]]))
  )
}))
bp_frame$Segmentation <- factor(
  bp_frame$Segmentation,
  levels = rev(c("Reference truth", names(callers)))
)
bp_frame$row <- as.numeric(bp_frame$Segmentation)

tolerance <- 0.3 * Mb
ref_bp <- data.frame(pos = start(getSegmentBreakpoints(reference)))

ggplot() +
  geom_rect(
    data = ref_bp,
    aes(
      xmin = (pos - tolerance) / Mb, xmax = (pos + tolerance) / Mb,
      ymin = 0.4, ymax = 5.6
    ),
    fill = "#2B8CBE", alpha = 0.18
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = bp_frame, aes(x = pos / Mb, y = row),
    size = 3.5, colour = "#D7301F"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:5, labels = levels(bp_frame$Segmentation)) +
  labs(
    title = "Breakpoints, and the 300 kb window they have to land in",
    subtitle = "Blue bands are the tolerance windows around the true transitions",
    x = "Position on chr1 (Mb)"
  ) +
  theme_slide()
```

### How to use it

```{r boundary-use}
bind_rows(lapply(names(callers), function(nm) {
  b <- computeBoundaryConcordance(callers[[nm]], reference, tolerance_bp = 3e5)
  data.frame(
    Caller = nm,
    precision = round(b$boundary_precision, 3),
    recall = round(b$boundary_recall, 3),
    f1 = round(b$boundary_f1, 3),
    n_called = b$n_query_breakpoints
  )
}))
```

Read the two rates as a pair. Low precision with high recall is
over-segmentation: it found every real transition and a great many others. The
reverse is a caller that merges events.

### Choosing the tolerance

The default of 300 kb encodes a real claim: a breakpoint called within about
three bins of the truth *is* the same breakpoint, because no capture assay
localises a transition more precisely than the spacing of its targets. Tighten
it only if the grid genuinely supports it, and note the asymmetry -- a generous
tolerance flatters an over-segmented caller, because more of its spurious
breakpoints fall inside some window.

### When to use it

Whenever the boundary positions themselves matter: matching CNV ends to
structural-variant breakpoints, deciding whether an event is focal or arm-level,
or defining a region for downstream gene-level annotation.

### Advantages

* Completely state-blind, so it isolates the structural half of the problem. A
  caller scoring 1.0 here and near 0 on kappa has found the right transitions
  and mis-assigned every level -- a purity or ploidy problem, not a segmentation
  one.
* Precision and recall separately, so the direction of the error is visible.

### Limitations

* The score is meaningless without stating the tolerance, which is why the
  function echoes it back in its return value.
* Matching is done independently in each direction, so three query breakpoints
  crowded into one window all count as matched against a single reference
  breakpoint. That is deliberate -- the separate denominators are what stop
  crowding from being rewarded -- but it means `n_matched_query` and
  `n_matched_subject` can differ.
* Two empty breakpoint sets score a perfect 1.0. They genuinely do agree that
  the genome has no internal transitions, but this is worth knowing before
  reading that 1.0 as skill.

## `computeSegmentationARI()` -- do the two agree on what belongs together?

### What it measures

Treat each segmentation as a way of grouping bins: two bins are "together" if
the same segment contains them. The adjusted Rand index asks how often the two
segmentations agree about whether a *pair* of bins belongs together, corrected
for the agreement expected by chance. 1 is identical, 0 is no better than
random.

### Intuition

```{r fig-ari, fig.height = 4.2, fig.cap = "The adjusted Rand index counts pairs of bins the two segmentations agree to keep together or to separate. Bins A and B are together in the reference and apart for the caller, so they form a disagreeing pair; A and C are apart in both, so they agree."}
demo_ref <- makeSegmentation(c(0, 15, 30) * Mb, c("NEUT", "AMP"))
demo_frag <- makeSegmentation(
  c(0, 8, 15, 22, 30) * Mb,
  c("NEUT", "NEUT", "AMP", "AMP")
)
demo_points <- data.frame(
  pos = c(3, 11, 20) * Mb,
  label = c("Bin A", "Bin B", "Bin C")
)

plotTracks(list("Fragmented caller" = demo_frag, "Reference" = demo_ref),
  title = "Bin pairs, not bins"
) +
  geom_vline(
    data = demo_points, aes(xintercept = pos / Mb),
    linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey20"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = demo_points, aes(x = pos / Mb, y = 2.65, label = label),
    size = 4.6
  )
```

### How to use it

```{r ari-use}
bind_rows(lapply(names(callers), function(nm) {
  a_seg <- computeSegmentationARI(callers[[nm]], reference,
    bins = targets,
    partition_by = "segment"
  )
  a_state <- computeSegmentationARI(callers[[nm]], reference,
    bins = targets,
    partition_by = "state"
  )
  data.frame(
    Caller = nm,
    ari_segment = round(a_seg$ari, 3),
    ari_state = round(a_state$ari, 3),
    n_query_segments = a_seg$n_query_groups
  )
}))
```

The `partition_by` argument is the whole point and there is no sensible default
to hide it behind:

* `"segment"` (the default) labels each bin by **which segment contains it**. A
  caller that cleanly halves every reference segment, stating both halves
  correctly, scores about 0.5 -- right biology, wrong granularity, which is
  exactly what this mode is for.
* `"state"` labels each bin by its **copy-number state**. The same caller scores
  1.0. Use `computeStateKappa()` for that question instead; it is the standard
  statistic and its value has a direct reading, whereas an ARI over a state
  partition is a pair-counting quantity with no comparable interpretation.

### When to use it

When a single structural agreement number is needed and granularity matters --
comparing segmentation algorithms, or tuning a smoothing parameter.

### Advantages

* Chance-corrected, so it is not inflated by there being many segments.
* Sensitive to over- and under-segmentation in a way that state metrics
  structurally cannot be.
* Needs no state column at all in `"segment"` mode, so it works on segmentations
  that carry only coordinates.

### Limitations

* Symmetric: it reports that the two differ, never which is fragmented. Pair it
  with `computeFragmentation()`.
* Not a metric in the mathematical sense (no triangle inequality), so
  "caller A is closer to the truth than caller B" does not chain reliably.
  `computeSegmentationVI()` does have that property.
* The value depends on the bin grid, so only compare ARIs computed on the same
  grid. This is why the auto-tiled grid here is derived from the genome rather
  than from the coordinate range of the inputs.

## `computeSegmentationVI()` -- an information-theoretic distance

### What it measures

Variation of information: having been told one segmentation, how much is still
unknown about the other?

$$VI(A, B) = H(A) + H(B) - 2\,I(A;B)$$

Lower is better; 0 means identical. Unlike ARI it is a true metric -- symmetric,
and obeying the triangle inequality -- and, more usefully, it **decomposes**.
The `h_query - mi` term is information the caller has that the reference does
not (over-segmentation); `h_subject - mi` is the reverse (under-segmentation).

### Intuition

```{r fig-vi, fig.height = 4.6, fig.cap = "Variation of information splits into the part of the disagreement caused by splitting and the part caused by merging. Total bar length is the variation of information; the split says which direction the error runs."}
vi_tbl <- bind_rows(lapply(names(callers), function(nm) {
  v <- computeSegmentationVI(callers[[nm]], reference, bins = targets)
  data.frame(
    Caller = nm,
    `Excess detail in the caller (splitting)` = v$h_query - v$mi,
    `Detail lost by the caller (merging)` = v$h_subject - v$mi,
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}))
vi_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(vi_tbl, -Caller,
  names_to = "Component",
  values_to = "Nats"
)
vi_long$Caller <- factor(vi_long$Caller, levels = rev(names(callers)))

ggplot(vi_long, aes(x = Nats, y = Caller, fill = Component)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#D7301F", "#2B8CBE")) +
  labs(
    title = "The two halves of a segmentation disagreement",
    x = "Variation of information (nats)"
  ) +
  theme_slide() +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

### How to use it

```{r vi-use}
v <- computeSegmentationVI(fragmented, reference, bins = targets)
c(
  vi = round(v$vi, 3), nvi = round(v$nvi, 3),
  over = round(v$h_query - v$mi, 3), under = round(v$h_subject - v$mi, 3)
)
```

**Use `nvi`, not `vi`, for anything comparative.** Raw VI is unbounded and grows
with the number of bins, so a VI of 1.2 on a 3,000-bin grid and a VI of 1.2 on a
200,000-bin grid mean quite different things, and averaging raw VI across
samples whose grids differ is meaningless. `nvi` divides by `log(n_bins)`, the
maximum attainable, giving a `[0, 1]` quantity that can be averaged.

### When to use it

When distances that behave like distances are needed -- clustering
segmentations, building a dendrogram of callers, or embedding a parameter sweep
-- and when the over/under decomposition is wanted for free.

### Advantages

* A true metric, so distances compose.
* Decomposes cleanly into the two directions of error.
* Well behaved when the two segmentations have very different numbers of
  segments, where ARI can be erratic.

### Limitations

* Measured in nats, which nobody has an intuition for. A VI of 0.4 is not
  self-explanatory the way a kappa of 0.4 is.
* Not chance-corrected in the way ARI is; two random partitions do not score a
  fixed value.
* Raw `vi` is not comparable across grids. Use `nvi`.

## `computeFragmentation()` -- which way does the disagreement run?

### What it measures

ARI and VI both say two segmentations differ; `computeFragmentation()` says
whether the caller is splitting the reference or merging it, and by how much.

### Intuition

```{r fig-frag, fig.height = 4.4, fig.cap = "How many caller segments meet a single reference segment. Above one is splitting; the conservative caller sits below one on the reverse measure, meaning it merges. The dashed line is a one-to-one correspondence between the two segmentations."}
frag_tbl <- bind_rows(lapply(names(callers), function(nm) {
  f <- computeFragmentation(callers[[nm]], reference, bins = targets)
  data.frame(
    Caller = nm,
    `Caller segments per reference segment` = f$mean_query_per_subject,
    `Reference segments per caller segment` = f$mean_subject_per_query,
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}))
frag_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(frag_tbl, -Caller,
  names_to = "Direction",
  values_to = "Mean"
)
frag_long$Caller <- factor(frag_long$Caller, levels = rev(names(callers)))

ggplot(frag_long, aes(x = Mean, y = Caller, fill = Direction)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.65) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#D7301F", "#2B8CBE")) +
  labs(
    title = "Splitting or merging?",
    x = "Mean number of partner segments (bin-weighted)"
  ) +
  theme_slide() +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

### How to use it

```{r frag-use}
f <- computeFragmentation(fragmented, reference, bins = targets)
f[c(
  "split_ratio", "merge_ratio",
  "mean_query_per_subject", "mean_subject_per_query"
)]
```

`mean_query_per_subject` is the average number of distinct caller segments
overlapping one reference segment, weighted by bins. A value of 2 means the
caller cuts each reference segment in half on average; 1 means one-to-one; below
1 is not attainable, since a reference segment always meets at least one caller
segment among its scorable bins.

`split_ratio` and `merge_ratio` are plain segment-count ratios. They react
faster but ignore how much genome each segment covers, so read them together: a
`split_ratio` of 5 with a `mean_query_per_subject` of 1.1 is a caller adding
many tiny segments in *one place*, not fragmenting throughout.

### When to use it

Immediately after ARI or VI shows that the segmentations differ, and always when
tuning a sensitivity or smoothing parameter -- this is the number that indicates
which way to turn it.

### Advantages

* Directional and blunt: it can be acted on without further interpretation.
* Computed on bins, so a segment sitting over an unsequenced region does not
  count as evidence of fragmentation.

### Limitations

* Not normalised to `[0, 1]` and not chance-corrected, so it ranks nothing on
  its own.
* Averages hide locality. A genome that is perfect everywhere except one
  shattered chromosome looks mildly fragmented throughout.

# Part 4 -- Which individual segments can be trusted?

Parts 2 and 3 reduce a whole segmentation to a handful of numbers. That is what
is needed to *choose* a caller; it is useless for the question that comes next,
which is which of the chosen caller's segments to believe. These functions
attach the comparison to each segment, so the segmentation can be filtered
rather than accepted or rejected whole.

## `annotateBinStateConcordance()` -- per-segment state accuracy

### What it measures

For each segment, the fraction of its targets whose state matches what the
reference says about the same targets. Size-neutral: a two-target segment that
is entirely right scores 1, the same as a two-thousand-target one.

### Intuition

Laid out like Figure 1 -- the truth on top, the callers underneath -- but with
each segment shaded by its own score rather than by its state. Every caller is
wrong in a different place, and the picture says where.

```{r fig-conc, fig.height = 6.4, fig.cap = "Per-segment state concordance for all four callers against the reference. Green segments state the copy number correctly over their targets; red ones do not. The spurious neutral gap the fragmented caller inserted inside the amplification is the single red block on its row."}
conc_scored <- lapply(callers, function(x) {
  annotateBinStateConcordance(x, reference, bins = targets)
})

scoredTrackFigure(
  conc_scored,
  score_col = "state.concordance",
  score_name = "State concordance",
  title = "Per-segment state accuracy, caller by caller",
  subtitle = "Each segment shaded by the fraction of its targets whose state is correct"
)
```

Read it row by row. The **accurate caller** is uniformly green: every segment
states the right level over its own targets. The **fragmented caller** is almost
all green too -- and that is the point of a size-neutral score, because its
shards are individually correct even though the segmentation as a whole is
over-cut; only the invented neutral gap at 9.2-9.9 Mb goes red. The
**conservative caller** shows the opposite pattern: its huge final segment is a
middling yellow-green, because it is right over the neutral stretches and wrong
over the whole deletion it missed. The **shifted caller** degrades gently
everywhere, which is the signature of correct events at wrong coordinates.

### How to use it

```{r conc-use}
frag_scored <- conc_scored[["Fragmented caller"]]

head(as.data.frame(mcols(frag_scored)), 4)
```

Three columns are attached: `state.concordance` (the fraction),
`state.n_matched` and `state.n_total`. The counters matter -- they are what
aggregates correctly. Pooling `state.n_matched` over `state.n_total` gives the
target-weighted accuracy of the whole segmentation; averaging the per-segment
fractions gives every segment an equal vote. Both are useful, they are not the
same number, and `summariseStateConcordance()` reports each.

The function is **directional**, and both directions are worth computing:

* caller against reference behaves like a precision -- of what this segment
  claims, how much is right;
* reference against caller behaves like a recall -- of what was really there,
  how much was found.

### When to use it

To filter. Drop or flag the segments that score badly, keep the rest, and carry
on with a partially trustworthy call set rather than throwing the sample away.
Also as the input to `computeEventRecovery()`, which is built on top of it.

### Advantages

* Size-neutral, so a small correct segment is not swamped by a large one.
* Returns a `GRanges` with new `mcols`, following the same convention as
  `compareSegmentOverlap()`, so it drops straight into an existing workflow.
* Hoistable: pass a precomputed `reference_state` from `assignBinState()` when
  scoring many segmentations against one reference.

### Limitations

* A segment with no target carrying a defined reference state gets `NA`, not 0.
  These are genuinely different -- "nothing to score against" versus "had
  targets and got them all wrong" -- and conflating them when aggregating will
  quietly reward callers that place segments in deserts.
* Blind to position: a segment can score 1.0 while sitting well away from the
  reference segment it agrees with. Pair it with `annotateBinJaccard()`.

## `annotateBinJaccard()` -- per-segment positional overlap

### What it measures

For every segment on **both** sides, the Jaccard overlap with its best-matching
counterpart, measured in targets rather than base pairs, together with that
counterpart's state and the three counts the score is built from.

Measuring in targets is the point. On capture data the base-pair extent of a
segment is dominated by the unsequenced gaps it spans, so a base-pair Jaccard
behaves largely as a segment-length metric and rewards a caller for placing
boundaries in deserts where no evidence exists. Counting targets measures the
evidence that was actually available.

### Intuition

Again in the layout of Figure 1. Compare this figure with the concordance one
above: the two score the *same* segmentations on unrelated criteria, and the
rows that look good here are not the rows that looked good there.

```{r fig-jaccard-tracks, fig.height = 6.4, fig.cap = "Best target-set Jaccard for each segment against its best-matching reference partner. The fragmented caller scores poorly everywhere despite being state-correct everywhere, because each of its shards covers only a fraction of the reference segment it matches."}
jac_scored <- lapply(callers, function(x) {
  annotateBinJaccard(x, reference, bins = targets)$query
})

scoredTrackFigure(
  jac_scored,
  score_col = "bin.jaccard.index",
  score_name = "Best target Jaccard",
  title = "Per-segment positional overlap, caller by caller",
  subtitle = "Grey would mark a segment with no overlapping counterpart"
)
```

This is the figure that shows why the two per-segment annotators must be read
together. The **fragmented caller** was almost entirely green in the concordance
figure and is almost entirely orange here: every shard names the right copy
number, and no shard covers its reference segment. Conversely the
**conservative caller**'s first segment is a solid green -- it overlaps the
neutral reference stretch well -- while the amplification it does report is a
poor positional match. A caller can be trusted on state and not on extent, or
the reverse, and one number cannot express that.

### The counts behind the score

```{r fig-jaccard, fig.height = 4.8, fig.cap = "The three target counts distinguish a merge from a split, which the Jaccard alone cannot."}
jac <- annotateBinJaccard(fragmented, reference, bins = targets)
jac_df <- as.data.frame(jac$query)
jac_df$segment <- sprintf("%.1f-%.1f Mb", jac_df$start / Mb, jac_df$end / Mb)
jac_df$segment <- factor(jac_df$segment, levels = rev(jac_df$segment))

counts_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(
  jac_df,
  cols = c("bin.jaccard.n_self", "bin.jaccard.n_match", "bin.jaccard.n_shared"),
  names_to = "Count", values_to = "Targets"
)
counts_long$Count <- factor(
  counts_long$Count,
  levels = c("bin.jaccard.n_self", "bin.jaccard.n_match", "bin.jaccard.n_shared"),
  labels = c("In this caller segment", "In its best reference partner", "Shared")
)

ggplot(counts_long, aes(x = Targets, y = segment, fill = Count)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#D7301F", "#2B8CBE", "grey40")) +
  labs(
    title = "Reading the target counts of the fragmented caller",
    subtitle = "Own count far below the partner's = a split. Far above it = a merge.",
    x = "Number of capture targets"
  ) +
  theme_slide() +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

### How to use it

```{r jaccard-use}
head(as.data.frame(mcols(jac$query))[, c(
  "cnv.annotation", "bin.jaccard.index",
  "bin.jaccard.status",
  "bin.jaccard.n_self",
  "bin.jaccard.n_match",
  "bin.jaccard.n_shared"
)], 5)
```

Three ways to score low, distinguished by the counts:

* `n_self` much greater than `n_match` -- this segment swallowed several
  counterparts: a **merge**, wanting more sensitivity.
* `n_self` much less than `n_match` -- this segment is one shard of a
  counterpart: a **split**, wanting less.
* both similar with a small `n_shared` -- the segments are simply in different
  places.

`bin.jaccard.status` carries the state of the winning counterpart, so a segment
with a good overlap but a mismatched status has found the right region and the
wrong copy number.

### When to use it

Whenever per-segment confidence is needed for downstream reporting -- flagging
which gene-level calls rest on a well-matched segment, for instance. Use it
alongside `annotateBinStateConcordance()`: this one rewards positional overlap
and is indifferent to state, the other is the opposite.

### Advantages

* Annotates both sides in one call, so unmatched reference segments (missed
  events) and unmatched caller segments (invented ones) are both visible.
* Target-based, so it is not fooled by capture deserts.
* Single bin assignment means `n_self + n_match - n_shared` is a true set union;
  counting overlaps instead would count a boundary-straddling target twice.

### Limitations

* A segment with no overlapping counterpart gets `NA`, flagged as
  `"NO_OVERLAP"`. For per-segment inspection that is correct; for an average it
  is a genuine zero, and `summariseSegmentJaccard()` treats it as one while
  separately reporting how often it happened.
* Best-match only. A segment split evenly across two counterparts is scored
  against one of them.
* Entirely state-blind in the score itself.

## `computeBreakpointConsistency()` and `annotateBreakpointConsistency()`

### What they measure

These two are the bridge into Part 5: they need no reference at all.
`computeBreakpointConsistency()` takes a *family* of segmentations of the same
sample -- several callers, or the same caller at several settings -- clusters
their boundaries, and reports for each cluster the fraction of the family that
places a boundary there. `annotateBreakpointConsistency()` then attaches those
recurrence scores back onto the boundaries of any one segmentation.

### Intuition

Because this metric needs no reference, the natural picture is the whole family
at once: the segment tracks of Figure 1 on top, and underneath, how much of the
family votes for each boundary cluster.

```{r fig-consistency, fig.height = 6.6, fig.cap = "Boundaries every caller agrees on are almost certainly real transitions. Boundaries only one caller reports are usually artefacts of its settings. The dotted verticals carry the cluster positions up through the tracks; the blue dashed lines in the lower panel are the true transitions, shown only for orientation -- the score never sees them."}
consistency <- computeBreakpointConsistency(callers, tolerance_bp = 3e5)

track_top <- plotTracks(
  c(list("Reference truth" = reference), callers),
  title = "Where the family agrees a boundary belongs",
  subtitle = wrapSub("Lower panel: the fraction of the four callers placing a boundary in each cluster")
) +
  geom_vline(
    data = consistency, aes(xintercept = pos / Mb),
    colour = "grey35", linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  xlim_chr + labs(x = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), plot.margin = margin(b = 2))

cons_bottom <- ggplot(consistency, aes(x = pos / Mb, y = consistency)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = consistency), width = 0.35) +
  geom_vline(
    data = data.frame(pos = start(getSegmentBreakpoints(reference))),
    aes(xintercept = pos / Mb), linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "#2B8CBE", linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "#FDD0A2", high = "#00441B",
    limits = c(0, 1), guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  xlim_chr +
  labs(x = "Position on chr1 (Mb)", y = "Callers") +
  theme_slide() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 90), plot.margin = margin(t = 2))

track_top / cons_bottom + plot_layout(heights = c(5, 2), guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Fifteen clusters come out, and the split is instructive. Ten sit at 0.25 -- each
the private invention of a single caller: six from the fragmented caller (3.4,
9.2, 9.9, 15.5, 21.0 and 26.2 Mb), three from the shifted caller (5.4, 20.6,
24.4 Mb) and one from the conservative caller (8.5 Mb). Those are the boundaries
to drop.

Five clusters reach 0.5, the ceiling for this family, and **four** of them sit on
a true transition -- 7.175, 12.85, 19.125 and 22.85 Mb, each carried by the
accurate and fragmented callers together. So far the metric is doing exactly what
it promises.

The fifth is the one to study. The cluster at **11.4 Mb is not a transition at
all**: it is where the conservative caller ends its truncated amplification
(11.5 Mb) and the shifted caller ends its displaced one (11.3 Mb). Two
independent callers, two different failure modes, one coincidental agreement --
and it scores just as highly as the four genuine transitions. This is the
limitation at the end of this section made concrete, and it is worth internalising
before using consistency to filter anything: the score cannot distinguish a
boundary that is reproducible because it is real from one that is reproducible
because two callers happen to be wrong in the same place.

### How to use it

```{r consistency-use}
consistency

ann <- annotateBreakpointConsistency(accurate, consistency, tolerance_bp = 3e5)
ann$summary
```

Clustering walks the sorted positions on each chromosome and opens a new cluster
whenever the next position is further than `tolerance_bp` from the **running
median** of the open one. Using the median rather than the last position is what
stops a chain of closely spaced boundaries from merging into one cluster of
unbounded width. Each segmentation contributes at most one vote per cluster, so
a caller that shatters a region cannot manufacture support for it.

### When to use it

On real samples, where no truth exists. A segmentation built mostly out of
idiosyncratic boundaries is over-fitted to its parameters, and its mean
consistency says so before any truth is consulted. Also as a map: the unanimous
clusters are the transitions the data forces regardless of setting, and are the
safest coordinates to hand to downstream analysis.

### Advantages

* Needs no ground truth.
* Works both as a genome-wide map and as a per-segment annotation.
* Cheap -- it only touches boundary coordinates, not bins.

### Limitations

* **Recurrence is agreement, not correctness.** If most members of the family
  share a failure mode -- and settings of the same algorithm frequently do -- a
  wrong boundary can be perfectly consistent. Treat a high score as the absence
  of one specific defect, not as evidence of quality.
* Sensitive to family composition. Three variants of one algorithm plus one
  independent one is not a panel of four opinions.
* Sensitive to `tolerance_bp`, which must match between the two functions.

# Part 5 -- No truth available: comparing callers to each other

Everything above needs a reference known to be right, which in practice means
simulated data. The two functions here compare a family of segmentations to each
other, so they run on real samples.

The same caveat applies to both, and it is important enough to repeat: **at very
low purity every caller agrees that nothing happened, and every caller is
wrong.** The maximum agreement score is produced both by an easy sample and by
an impossible one. High agreement is evidence of quality only conditional on the
sample being solvable at all, and that has to be established separately -- from
purity, coverage and noise.

For this reason the vocabulary here is deliberately different: the pairwise
quantity is called `overlap` rather than `jaccard`, and nothing is called recall
or precision. These are caller-versus-caller quantities with no reference
involved, and naming them like the truth-based metrics would let a consensus
number pass for an achieved-quality one.

## `computeCallerAgreement()` -- do the callers see the same thing?

### What it measures

Tiles the genome, asks every caller whether each bin is altered, and summarises
how much the answers coincide. Where `computeBreakpointConsistency()` asks
whether the callers cut in the same places, this asks whether they agree about
what is there.

### Intuition

```{r fig-agreement, fig.height = 4.6, fig.cap = "Pairwise agreement on which targets are altered. The callers that find both events agree with each other; the conservative caller, which misses the deletion, sits apart from all of them."}
ag <- computeCallerAgreement(callers, bins = targets)

pairs_sym <- bind_rows(
  ag$pairwise[, c("method_a", "method_b", "overlap")],
  data.frame(
    method_a = ag$pairwise$method_b,
    method_b = ag$pairwise$method_a,
    overlap = ag$pairwise$overlap
  ),
  data.frame(method_a = names(callers), method_b = names(callers), overlap = 1)
)

ggplot(pairs_sym, aes(x = method_a, y = method_b, fill = overlap)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", overlap)), size = 5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "grey95", high = "#2B8CBE", limits = c(0, 1),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "How much the callers agree about the altered genome",
    subtitle = "Overlap of the sets of targets each pair calls altered. No truth is involved.",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_slide() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )
```

### How to use it

```{r agreement-use}
ag$summary
```

`agree_frac_majority` is the fraction of targets more than half the callers call
altered -- a rough consensus altered fraction. `agree_vote_entropy_mean` is the
per-target vote entropy: zero when the callers are unanimous either way, maximal
when they split down the middle. A high entropy is the clearest signal that a
sample is genuinely ambiguous rather than merely difficult for one caller.

### When to use it

As a per-sample QC flag on real cohorts, and as the natural companion to
`computeBreakpointConsistency()`. Low agreement combined with adequate purity
and coverage is a sample worth looking at by hand.

### Advantages

* No ground truth needed, so it runs on every real sample available.
* Reports the pairwise detail as well as the summary, so an outlier caller is
  identifiable rather than merely averaged in.
* The entropy term distinguishes "everyone is confidently wrong together" from
  "the callers are split".

### Limitations

* Agreement is not monotone with quality; see the caveat opening this section.
* Reduces states to altered/not, discarding the amplification versus deletion
  distinction entirely.
* Callers sharing a code lineage will agree with each other for reasons that
  have nothing to do with the data.

## `computeConsensusAgreement()` -- which caller is the odd one out?

### What it measures

For every caller, how well its altered regions match the majority verdict of the
**other** callers. The consensus is computed leave-one-out, so a caller is never
scored against a consensus it helped define.

### Intuition

```{r fig-consensus, fig.height = 4.6, fig.cap = "Two directional scores that must be read as a pair: how much of the peers' consensus a caller recovers, and how much of its own output the peers back. Leave-one-out, so no caller is scored against a consensus it helped build."}
loo <- computeConsensusAgreement(callers, bins = targets)

ggplot(loo, aes(
  x = loo_consensus_captured, y = loo_consensus_supported,
  label = method
)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = altered_rate), colour = "#D7301F") +
  geom_text(vjust = -1.6, size = 4.6) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(3, 9), name = "Fraction of genome called altered") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.25, 1.25)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.05, 1.20)) +
  annotate("text",
    x = 1.0, y = 0.08, label = "over-calling",
    colour = "grey40", size = 4.5
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = 0.15, y = 1.1, label = "under-calling",
    colour = "grey40", size = 4.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Each caller against the consensus of the others",
    x = "Share of the peers' consensus this caller recovers",
    y = "Share of this caller's calls the peers back"
  ) +
  theme_slide() +
  theme(axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 90), legend.title = element_text())
```

### How to use it

```{r consensus-use}
loo[
  order(-loo$loo_consensus_overlap),
  c(
    "method", "loo_consensus_overlap", "loo_mean_pairwise",
    "loo_consensus_captured", "loo_consensus_supported", "altered_rate"
  )
]
```

`loo_consensus_overlap` merges both directions into one symmetric number and
cannot distinguish them; the two directional columns can. Always read
`altered_rate` alongside them -- a caller that calls nothing altered has an
uninterpretable pair of directional scores.

`loo_mean_pairwise` is the mean overlap against each other caller taken
individually. It is less brittle than the consensus when the peers disagree
among themselves, and with a small family it is often the more informative of
the two.

### Why it does not use `findConsensus()`

`findConsensus()` and `ensemblCall()` merge segments and fill gaps, which
changes the geometry: the result is not the set of regions the peers agreed on
but a post-processed segmentation of it. Comparing against that would silently
mix "do the callers agree" with "does merging help". A bin vote is used instead,
which is also several orders of magnitude faster to rebuild once per caller.

### When to use it

As a truth-free selection signal on real samples: absent a shared failure mode,
the output that best matches what everyone else independently found is more
likely to be right. Also as a caller-level QC across a cohort -- a caller that is
consistently the outlier is worth investigating.

### Advantages

* Leave-one-out, so it does not reward typicality inconsistently in proportion
  to how much each caller contributed to the thing it is scored against.
* Directional, so over- and under-calling are distinguishable.
* Fast enough to run on every sample in a cohort.

### Limitations

* With only two callers the "consensus" is the other caller, and the metric
  degenerates into a pairwise overlap.
* With three callers the peer consensus requires both peers to agree, since a
  strict majority of two is two. This is the right choice -- a tie is precisely
  the case where there is no consensus -- but it makes the score conservative.
* Rewards the mainstream. A caller that is right where everyone else is wrong
  scores badly, by construction.

# Part 6 -- Whole-profile comparison on `cnvstrml` objects

Everything so far has worked on bare `GRanges` and measured agreement over an
evidence grid. The functions in this part take `cnvstrml` objects instead and
measure agreement in **base pairs**. That difference is not cosmetic, and the
first thing to be clear about is when each is appropriate:

* **Target-based** (Parts 2 to 5). Counts only the genome the assay could see.
  Correct for capture and amplicon data, where most of the genome carries no
  evidence.
* **Base-pair based** (this part). Counts every base equally, including the ones
  nobody sequenced. Correct for whole-genome data, and actively misleading on a
  capture panel, where it rewards a caller for spanning deserts.

These also read allele copy numbers and log-ratios, so they can say things the
bin metrics cannot -- which *state* was confused, and how much of the altered
genome was recovered.
